summary: This Itamar Medical article discusses a 2021 study by Antonaglia and Passuti on obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in nonobese patients, focusing on the role of low respiratory arousal threshold (LRAT). It explains that LRAT is present in 30% to 50% of OSA patients, that nonobese OSA patients face notable cardiovascular risks such as hypertension and early atherosclerosis, and that low arousal threshold is linked to poorer CPAP adherence. The authors call for further pathophysiologic studies to clarify LRAT's role in nonobese OSA.
one_line: Article on how low respiratory arousal threshold (LRAT) may explain difficulty treating obstructive sleep apnea in nonobese patients.
key_facts: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a disease that is also a risk factor for many other health problems.
Anatomical predisposition factors are present in all OSA patients, and 70% of cases involve one or more associated non-anatomical pathophysiologic factors.

The four pathophysiologic factors in OSA are anatomic collapse of the upper airways, instability of ventilatory control (high loop gain), neuromuscular inefficiency of the upper airway dilator muscles, and increased propensity for nocturnal awakenings due to low arousal threshold.
Low arousal threshold is also called low respiratory arousal threshold, or LRAT.
Low arousal threshold is present in 30% to 50% of all patients with OSA.
LRAT was observed in more than 60% of African American patients evaluated for OSA in a study by Moghalu, Whitesell and Kwagyan.
Nonobese patients are defined as those with a BMI below 30 kg/m2.
Approximately 20% of adults with OSA are nonobese.
The number of people with OSA in the United States is thought to be as many as 18 million, or 1 in 15 adults, with 80% undiagnosed.
Nonobese patients with OSA are 4 times more likely to develop hypertension than obese individuals without OSA.
Nonobese patients are at risk for early atherosclerosis, approximately 2.7 times more than obese patients without OSA, and this risk increases as OSA severity increases.
Nonobese patients with OSA are usually younger, so early detection and care could reduce long-term risk.
Nonobese patients with OSA with a low arousal threshold have poorer adherence to CPAP therapy.
Non-anatomic interventions such as non-myorelaxant sedatives may yield greater therapeutic success in nonobese patients, alone or combined with CPAP or oral appliances.

Polysomnography (PSG) is routinely indicated for diagnosing respiratory sleep disorders, and nocturnal portable monitoring (PM), often known as home sleep apnea tests (HSATs), is an excellent alternative.
